extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, regulators, and researchers interested in automotive emissions, corporate misconduct, and regulatory responses
extracted.subtask_description: Comprehensive Wikipedia-style article documenting the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' emissions scandal: technical findings, regulatory investigations and actions (EPA, CARB, DOJ, SEC), litigation and settlements, affected models, industry and market impacts, and calls for testing/regulatory reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU5 emissions standard compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to vehicles meeting 'EU5 standards' in testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes VW statements that 'the vehicles did meet EU5 standards, so it clearly contributed to meeting the EU5 standards in testing' — but highlights that such laboratory compliance can be the result of software that alters emissions during tests (i.e., defeat devices), so lab-based compliance alone may not indicate real-world compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits for nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist statutory/legal limits for NOx emissions that vehicles must not exceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real-world tests showed emissions from diesel engines up to 14 times higher than claimed, with every tested vehicle exceeding legal NOx limits. Compliance assessments should compare measured real-world NOx to applicable legal thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prohibition of 'defeat device' / test-cycle detection software
rubrics_metrics.description: Software or devices that detect test cycles and alter emissions controls to reduce emissions only during testing (a 'defeat device').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only Volkswagen Group vehicles were found to have test-cycle detection software in the cited investigations. Use of such devices is treated as deception that can trigger regulatory, civil, and criminal liability; regulators (EPA, CARB) and courts treat these devices as unlawful when they evade emissions standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-world on-road testing (PEMS) and adoption of WLTP
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that testing regimes reflect real driving conditions, e.g., Worldwide Harmonized Light vehicles Test Procedures (WLTP) and on-road testing via PEMS (portable emissions measurement systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers criticized laboratory-only tests (FTP-75) and called for WLTP and PEMS because they better reflect real-life driving. The new tests began to come into force in 2017, although industry lobbying delayed implementation according to critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory adequacy of recall plans (CARB standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall or remedy proposals submitted by a manufacturer must 'adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CARB rejected Volkswagen's December 2015 recall plans for affected 2.0‑litre diesel engines on the grounds that they did not adequately address these overall impacts, illustrating that regulators evaluate fixes beyond merely reducing emissions in test conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean Air Act liability and civil penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. federal law (Clean Air Act) manufacturers can face substantial per-vehicle penalties and aggregate liability for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA announced potential fines up to US$37,500 per vehicle (cited) and DOJ sought up to $46 billion in penalties in litigation. Regulators characterized hidden pollution as 'knowing endangerment', which can heighten liability and criminal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misleading advertising and use of devices to manipulate emissions tests (FTC/DOJ requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory orders can require cessation of misleading advertising and bar use of devices intended to manipulate emission tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FTC and DOJ mandated Volkswagen cease misleading advertising and prohibited use of devices intended to manipulate emissions tests; such prohibitions were folded into consolidated litigation and settlement terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer settlement remedy standards (buyback vs. repair and compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer remedies in class settlements may offer buyback, approved repair (fix), and monetary compensation with specified valuation methods and payout ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. settlement offered consumers choices: buyback (values $12,475–$44,176 depending on mileage/book value), EPA‑approved fixes with compensation ranges ($5,100–$9,852), and independent legal recourse if offers declined. Settlement also included restrictions (e.g., VW agreed not to resell/export repurchased vehicles unless an approved emission repair was completed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental mitigation and directed investment obligations in settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlements may require payments for environmental mitigation and directed spending to promote zero‑emission vehicles and infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volkswagen agreed to pay $2.7 billion for environmental mitigation and $2 billion for clean-emissions infrastructure, administered via a subsidiary (Electrify America) with defined installment schedules and subject to CARB and EPA approval and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory investigative protocol and scope expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators may broaden probes, sample used vehicles, and expand focus if suspicious data emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA broadened its probe to 28 diesel-powered models, initially focusing on one used vehicle per model and widening the probe upon encountering suspicious data. This illustrates a pragmatic investigative protocol for emissions compliance enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal culpability standards and enforcement (DOJ precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and corporations may face criminal investigations and charges (conspiracy to defraud, obstruction) when actions demonstrate knowing deception to regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include engineer plea deals admitting intentional installation of defeat devices, arrest and charges of managers, corporate guilty pleas (VW pleaded guilty to conspiracy and obstruction), and large criminal fines (e.g., $2.8B criminal fine cited), demonstrating the threshold and consequences for criminal enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securities and investor disclosure liability (SEC standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies and executives can be liable under securities laws for making false or misleading statements to investors and markets about product quality and regulatory compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEC filed a complaint alleging VW and its former CEO defrauded investors by selling securities while making false/misleading statements about vehicle quality and compliance; investor lawsuits and rating downgrades followed, showing investor-protection standards apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of market and resale impacts as indicators of scandal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Market metrics (share price changes, sales volumes, resale values) are valid measures of the scandal's economic and reputational impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents stock price drops, sales declines in certain markets, and used car resale value declines (5–16% depending on model), which were used to quantify financial consequences and justify writedowns and investor actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial consolidation and mass‑litigation procedural standard (MDL)
rubrics_metrics.description: When many related class actions arise, courts may consolidate into a multidistrict litigation (MDL) to coordinate proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated over 500 class actions into MDL No. 2672, illustrating the procedural standard for handling large-scale, related litigation efficiently and appointing leadership for plaintiffs' counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent testing and compliance benchmarks (examples from ADAC, national studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent, third-party testing programs provide compliance benchmarks and can reveal industry-wide noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple national studies (ADAC, French, German tests) found many diesel cars exceed legal NOx limits in normal driving (some by >10x), indicating independent testing is a necessary complement to manufacturer-provided test data and regulatory certification.
